summary:
We built Solaris, an interactive 3D space platform that brings NASA mission data for every planet in our solar system to life. Designed for students ages 8 to 14, users can click any planet from Mercury to Neptune to see active spacecraft and retired hardware orbiting or resting there. Each mission opens a story log with real NASA photos, voice narration, and a timeline spanning from 1957 to today.

Most space archives are full of dense numbers and complex reports that are hard for young learners to read. We solved this by turning decades of planetary exploration into an easy visual story called Abandoned but Not Forgotten. Instead of raw data tables, students experience each mission as a step by step journey.

Space exploration is a shared human adventure across many worlds. By bringing every planet and mission together in one interactive place, Solaris makes space history accessible and fun, inspiring the next generation of explorers.
details:
What It Does and How It Works Solaris is an interactive 3D web application that brings official NASA mission data for every planet in our solar system to life. Users begin by exploring a 3D solar system and can click on any planet from Mercury to Neptune. Selecting a planet opens a close up view showing the rotating planet, orbital paths, and both active spacecraft and retired hardware revolving around or resting on it. Clicking on any mission opens a Mission Recovery Log that combines real NASA photography, key mission facts like launch year and agency, step by step story chapters, and voice narration with an audio visualizer. An interactive timeline at the bottom lets users travel from 1957 to today to watch how planetary exploration unfolded over the decades.

Benefits Most official space data is stored in dense technical reports and complex tables that are difficult for young learners to read. Solaris turns decades of NASA archives into a visual, easy to follow experience in one unified place. Instead of focusing only on the Moon or Mars, users can explore the entire solar system and compare active probes with retired pioneers. Combining 3D graphics, real photography, short readable stories, and audio narration also supports different learning styles through both sight and sound.

Intended Impact Solaris is designed for students ages 8 to 14 to spark genuine curiosity about space exploration. Guided by the theme Abandoned but Not Forgotten, our goal is to show that retired spacecraft are not just old hardware left in space, but brave pioneers whose discoveries made modern missions possible. By making real space history accessible and engaging, we hope to inspire the next generation of young explorers, scientists, and engineers.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software Used We built Solaris as a modern web application using React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS for the user interface, alongside Framer Motion for smooth transitions. For the 3D solar system, rotating planets, and orbiting satellites, we used Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei. Our mission records were gathered and structured from official NASA planetary mission archives and real NASA image libraries. We developed and tested the platform on standard laptops using VS Code, Vite, pnpm, and GitHub for team collaboration.

How Our Project Is Creative Rather than building a standard encyclopedia or a data heavy dashboard, we designed Solaris like an interactive space recovery journal. We paired a warm copper and dark glass visual style with storytelling that feels adventurous without looking childish. Connecting a 1957 to 2026 time slider directly with live 3D orbits and voice narrated mission logs allows students to feel like they are uncovering real transmissions from deep space.

Factors Our Team Considered Our primary focus was designing for students ages 8 to 14. We avoided cluttered screens, complex orbital math, and heavy jargon so young users would stay engaged. At the same time, we avoided fake cartoon illustrations and used authentic NASA photos and accurate mission timelines so the experience feels real and respects their curiosity. We also carefully balanced the layout so the 3D planets and the story panels remain clean, readable, and responsive on standard web browsers.
